question: Open question: how do strong models perceive the knowledge boundaries of weak supervisors?
asked_by: Yang et al., Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
remaining_question: In Yang et al.'s weak-to-strong preference-alignment setup with a conflicting target, given that correctness of weak preference orders alone lets the strong model perceive weak-unknown samples, does it do so by checking each weak order against its own knowledge (as F2's stronger model predicting the weaker model's correctness suggests) or by inferring per-domain weak competence from the portion and distribution of supervised samples across domains, as would be tested by ablations that equalize the per-domain distribution while holding the correctness of the orders and the strong model fixed?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: In Yang et al.'s weak-to-strong preference-alignment setup, run ablations that equalize the per-domain distribution of supervised samples while holding the correctness of the weak orders and the strong model fixed, and see whether its perception of weak-unknown samples changes.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2604.25077v3: Evaluating Risks in Weak-to-Strong Alignment: A Bias-Variance Perspective
findings.claim: Across four weak-to-strong pipelines spanning SFT, RLHF and RLAIF on PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF, the authors find that, among the BVC quantities they study, strong-model variance is the one most strongly associated with 'blind-spot deception' (cases where the strong model is confidently wrong while the weak model is uncertain); covariance provides additional but weaker information, indicating that weak-strong dependence matters but does not by itself explain the observed failures. They treat a cross-dataset reversal as exploratory evidence for their claim that blind-spot deception also depends on how the weak model's training procedure shapes the regions where weak supervision is uncertain. They interpret the correlation results, based on only eight pipeline-dataset settings, as exploratory diagnostic evidence, and their experiments use only Llama-family models and harmlessness-style preference datasets.
findings.setting: Empirical; four weak-to-strong pipelines spanning SFT, RLHF and RLAIF on the harmlessness-style preference datasets PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF; only Llama-family models; correlations over eight pipeline-dataset settings. 'Deception' here is the blind-spot metric (strong model confidently wrong where the weak model is uncertain), not Yang et al.'s measure, so the result is not obtained in the question's own setup.
findings.bears_on: Whether strong-model errors in weak-unknown regions track weak-strong dependence (a perception channel) or the strong model's own confidence dispersion.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.24988v2: Generalized Correctness Models: Learning Calibrated and Model-Agnostic Correctness Predictors from Historical Patterns
findings.claim: The authors find that an LLM predicting the correctness of its own outputs generally does no better than an unrelated LLM, and hypothesise that exposure to a target model's historical predictions is key. When Qwen2.5-72B and Llama3-70B are finetuned on MMLU to predict each other's and their own correctness, Qwen2.5-72B predicts Llama3-70B's correctness, as well as its own, better than Llama3-70B does, which they attribute to Qwen2.5-72B being stronger with more knowledge of the true answers.
findings.setting: Correctness prediction trained with explicit correctness labels on MMLU; Qwen2.5-72B vs Llama3-70B (small capability gap); no weak-to-strong training and no conflicting objective.
findings.bears_on: Whether a stronger model can learn a weaker model's knowledge boundary from its track record and its own knowledge of the answers, one channel Yang et al. suggest.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2410.13787v1: Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
findings.claim: For GPT-4o, GPT-4 and Llama 70B, self-prediction models consistently outperform their cross-prediction counterparts on a set of held-out tasks: e.g. Llama 70B predicts its own behavior more accurately (48.5%) than GPT-4o does (31.8%), despite GPT-4o's superior capabilities, and GPT-4o predicts itself better (49.4%) than Llama 70B does (36.6%); GPT-3.5 has a statistically significant but very small (+0.8%) self-prediction advantage. In a data-scaling analysis, GPT-4o's cross-prediction of Llama 70B does not meaningfully increase after 10,000 samples and plateaus at 35.2%, far below the 48.5% self-prediction accuracy.
findings.setting: Self- vs cross-prediction finetuning among GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Llama 70B on held-out behavior-property tasks; predicts behavior properties, not knowledge or correctness; no weak-to-strong training.
findings.bears_on: Limits on how well a more capable model can model another model from observed behavior; contrasts with 2509.24988's finding for correctness.

passages.text:
Self-prediction models consistently outperform their cross-prediction counterparts for GPT-4o,
GPT-4, and Llama 70B on a set of held-out tasks, as shown in Figure 5. For instance, Llama
70B predicts its own behavior more accurately (48.5%) than GPT-4o (31.8%), despite GPT-4o’s
superior capabilities (Chiang et al., 2024). The same pattern holds the other way around: GPT-4o
predicts itself better (49.4%) than Llama 70B does (36.6%). GPT-3.5 has a statistically significant
but very small (+0.8%) self-prediction advantage (p = 0.002). For models other than GPT-3.5, the
self-prediction advantage holds across most datasets and behavior properties (see Figure 14). This
provides evidence that these models use introspection. Further evidence is that the self-prediction
advantage also holds on the set of tasks used in self-/cross-training (A.2.2).

Another possibility is that cross-prediction training requires more training samples and would eventually improve over self-prediction. We conduct a data-scaling analysis on GPT-4o predicting Llama
70B (Section A.2.7). Cross-prediction accuracy does not meaningfully increase after 10,000 samples: it plateaus at 35.2%, far below the self-prediction accuracy of 48.5%.
